feedback: If a child says the uneven three-colour spinner is fair 'because it has three colours', have them compare red against blue and green together: red covers as much as the other two combined, so it cannot have the same chance.
If a child says 'it's random, so every colour has an equal chance', note that an uneven spinner is still random yet lands on red far more often — random does not mean equally likely.
Praise reasoning that explicitly refers to equal size or equal counts rather than the number of colours.
activities.intendedInsight: Deciding fair vs not-fair is a categorisation grounded in comparing the size or number of each outcome; the sharpest traps are the three-colour uneven spinner ('three colours so equal') and the two-outcome cube ('two outcomes so 50-50').
learnerActions: Look at a set of chance devices — spinners with equal and unequal sections, a balanced coin, a balanced die, bags with equal and unequal numbers of each colour.
Sort each device into 'equally likely outcomes' or 'not equally likely'.
For a spinner that has three colours but with red filling half and blue and green each a quarter, decide whether the three colours are equally likely and explain why or why not.
For each device, give the reason that decided your answer — equal section size or equal counts, not the number of different colours.
Answer the trap question: 'A cube has one red face and five blue faces — there are two colours, so does that make red and blue equally likely?' Explain why not.
activities.title: Sort and decide: fair or not fair?

feedback: If the child accepts 'three colours so fair', prompt them to compare the sizes of the sections.
If the child conflates random with equally likely, ask: 'If we spun it 100 times, would the colours come up about the same? Why not?'
Confirm when the child names 'make the three sections the same size' as the fix.
activities.intendedInsight: Children can separate two ideas: an outcome being random (unpredictable on a single spin) versus outcomes being equally likely (same chance each). An uneven spinner is random but not equally likely.
learnerActions: Listen to a carnival host who insists a spinner with a big red section is 'totally fair — three colours, three chances'.
Explain to the host why having three colours does not make the colours equally likely.
Point out that red's section is bigger than the others, so red is more likely.

Address the host's fallback claim that 'it's random, so you can't say one colour is more likely' — explain that the spin is random but the colours are still NOT equally likely because the sections differ in size.
Say what the host would have to change to make the spinner genuinely fair (three equal-sized sections).
activities.title: Argue down the carnival host (equally likely vs random)
